clinicalPearls: Thrombocytopenia arises from one or more of three mechanisms: decreased bone marrow production, sequestration (usually in an enlarged spleen), and/or increased platelet destruction (Harrison 22e p.921).
First step in evaluating thrombocytopenia is reviewing the peripheral blood smear and ruling out pseudothrombocytopenia, especially when there is no apparent cause (Harrison 22e p.921).

Petechiae are pinpoint, nonblanching hemorrhages that usually signify a decreased platelet number rather than platelet dysfunction; they first appear in areas of increased venous pressure (ankles/feet in ambulatory patients) (Harrison 22e p.921-922).

Wet purpura (blood blisters on the oral mucosa) and retinal hemorrhages are thought to denote an increased risk of life-threatening hemorrhage in the thrombocytopenic patient (Harrison 22e p.922, 924).

Drugs are the most common cause of thrombocytopenia; in a patient with no apparent cause, all drugs (including herbal and OTC preparations) should be suspect and stopped or substituted if possible (Harrison 22e p.922).

Infection is the most common noniatrogenic cause of thrombocytopenia; viral and bacterial infections can affect both platelet production and survival, and immune mechanisms may also contribute (Harrison 22e p.921-922).
In HIT, thrombocytopenia is usually not severe (nadir rarely <20,000/uL) and is not associated with bleeding; instead it markedly increases the risk of thrombosis (Harrison 22e p.923).
Most patients develop HIT 5-14 days after heparin exposure; onset before 5 days suggests prior heparin exposure within ~100 days with circulating anti-heparin/PF4 antibodies (Harrison 22e p.923).
ITP is characterized by mucocutaneous bleeding and a low, often very low, platelet count with an otherwise normal peripheral blood smear and cell counts (Harrison 22e p.924).

In thrombotic microangiopathies (TTP/HUS) the PT and aPTT are characteristically normal, which helps distinguish them from DIC, where a coagulopathy predominates with elevated PT and often aPTT (Harrison 22e p.924-925).
An ADAMTS13 activity level of <10% is diagnostic of TTP (Harrison 22e p.925).

Markedly elevated platelet counts (>1.5 million), usually in a myeloproliferative disorder, carry an increased risk of bleeding rather than thrombosis, due in part to acquired von Willebrand disease (Harrison 22e p.926).
harrison.pathophysiology: Hemostasis depends on platelets and the vessel wall. Platelets are activated on adhesion to von Willebrand factor (VWF) and collagen in exposed subendothelium after injury; adhesion (primarily via VWF) generates signals activating the GpIIb/IIIa (alphaIIb-beta3) receptor and aggregation, with release of granule contents and stabilization by a fibrin mesh. Normal platelet count is 150,000-450,000/uL; thrombopoietin (TPO), made in the liver, is the major regulator, and roughly one-third of platelets reside in the spleen. Thrombocytopenia results from decreased production, splenic sequestration, and/or increased destruction. In HIT, antibodies form to a complex of platelet factor 4 (PF4) and heparin/glycosaminoglycans; the anti-heparin/PF4 antibody activates platelets via the FcgammaRIIa receptor and also activates monocytes, endothelium, and coagulation, producing a prothrombotic state. ITP is immune-mediated platelet destruction with possible inhibition of platelet release from megakaryocytes. In TTP, deficiency of or antibodies to the metalloprotease ADAMTS13 leave ultra-large VWF multimers uncleaved, driving pathogenic platelet adhesion/aggregation and microvascular thrombosis. HUS features acute renal failure with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia; atypical HUS arises from genetic complement-regulatory defects or anti-complement-regulator antibodies causing chronic complement activation.
additionalDifferentials: Decreased production (bone marrow disorders, myelodysplasia, chemotherapy-induced marrow suppression)
Inherited thrombocytopenia (e.g., MYH9-related autosomal dominant macrothrombocytopenia: May-Hegglin anomaly, Sebastian, Epstein, Fechtner syndromes)
Evans syndrome (combined autoimmune hemolytic anemia with ITP)
infectionMimics: Viral and bacterial infections causing thrombocytopenia (most common noniatrogenic cause)
Systemic gram-negative bacterial infection with DIC
Infectious mononucleosis and early HIV (immune-mediated thrombocytopenia)
Late HIV with pancytopenia and dysplastic platelet production
Hepatitis C and HIV as secondary causes of ITP
Helicobacter pylori (uncertain, geographically variable association with ITP)
nonInfectiousMimics: Pseudothrombocytopenia from EDTA-induced platelet clumping (in vitro artifact)
Iron deficiency, inflammation, or malignancy causing reactive thrombocytosis (when evaluating platelet count abnormalities)
Other microangiopathies: bone marrow transplant-associated, drug-induced, pregnancy-related, and vasculitis-associated
additionalInvestigations: Peripheral blood smear review (rule out clumping; assess RBC morphology and platelet size)
Repeat platelet count in sodium citrate (blue top) or heparin (green top) tube, or fresh fingerstick smear, if EDTA clumping suspected
Complete blood count with hemoglobin and white blood cell count
Bone marrow examination (isolated thrombocytopenia in patients >60 years or nonresponders to initial therapy)
4Ts scoring for HIT pretest probability (thrombocytopenia, timing, thrombosis/sequelae, other causes)
Anti-heparin/PF4 immunoassay (high sensitivity, low specificity) and serotonin release platelet-activation assay (lower sensitivity, higher specificity) for HIT
Lower extremity duplex Doppler imaging to evaluate for thrombosis in HIT
ADAMTS13 activity and inhibitor/antibody testing (activity <10% diagnostic of TTP)
LDH, unconjugated bilirubin, haptoglobin (evidence of hemolysis in MAHA)
PT and aPTT (normal in TTP/HUS; elevated in DIC)
Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test if anemia present (rule out Evans syndrome)
Secondary ITP workup: HIV, hepatitis C, SLE serology, serum protein electrophoresis, immunoglobulin levels, IgA deficiency / monoclonal gammopathy testing, H. pylori
Complement regulatory gene DNA variant testing for atypical HUS
redFlags: HIT: thrombosis (venous and/or arterial) despite a falling platelet count -- stop all heparin immediately (including LMWH, which cross-reacts) and start a non-heparin anticoagulant
Wet purpura (oral mucosal blood blisters) and retinal hemorrhages herald life-threatening, including CNS, bleeding
VITT: high D-dimer with thrombosis in unusual sites such as cerebral venous sinuses (fatal in ~20%)
New thrombocytopenia with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes) suggesting TTP -- a devastating disease if not promptly diagnosed and treated
Severe thrombocytopenia (<5000/uL) or signs of impending bleeding in ITP requiring urgent inpatient combined-modality therapy
Introducing warfarin alone in HIT/HITT may precipitate thrombosis (e.g., venous gangrene) due to reduced protein C and S
harrison.prognosis: ITP: in children usually acute, post-infectious, and self-limited; in adults more chronic, though some remit spontaneously within months. Patients with platelet counts >30,000/uL appear not to have increased mortality from the thrombocytopenia. TTP: introduction of plasma exchange reduced mortality from 85-100% to 10-30%; however 25-45% relapse within 30 days of remission and 12-40% have late relapses, with relapses more frequent in those with severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. HUS: diarrhea-associated HUS has overall mortality <5% (about 40% of children need dialysis), whereas non-diarrhea-associated HUS mortality is higher (~26%). VITT is fatal in about 20%.
pitfalls: Pseudothrombocytopenia: EDTA-induced platelet agglutination is an in vitro artifact and not true thrombocytopenia; confirm with a smear and a count in citrate/heparin or fresh fingerstick blood.
Anti-heparin/PF4 antibodies are common without clinical disease (e.g., ~50% after cardiopulmonary bypass), so the HIT immunoassay has low specificity; HIT remains a clinical diagnosis.
The 4T score is very useful for excluding HIT but overdiagnoses it in settings (e.g., ICU) where thrombocytopenia and thrombosis from other causes are common.
LMWH cross-reacts with HIT antibodies and must not be used to treat HIT.
Starting warfarin alone in HIT/HITT may precipitate thrombosis and venous gangrene; overlap with a DTI, fondaparinux, or DOAC and start only after thrombocytopenia resolves.
Serologic (antibody) testing in ITP is generally unhelpful due to low sensitivity and specificity.
Plasma infusion/exchange has not been shown to alter the overall course of HUS or atypical HUS (except aHUS with antibodies to factor H).
Petechiae indicate decreased platelet number, not platelet dysfunction -- excessive bruising can occur with disorders of either number or function.
harrison.severityClassification: No single formal grading scale is given; clinically meaningful thresholds noted: ~5000-10,000/uL platelets needed to maintain microvascular integrity; severe ITP thrombocytopenia <5000/uL (or impending bleeding) warrants inpatient combined-modality therapy; ITP counts >30,000/uL not associated with increased mortality; HIT nadir rarely <20,000/uL; ADAMTS13 activity <10% diagnostic of TTP; platelet counts >1.5 million (myeloproliferative) carry bleeding risk. The 4Ts score is used for HIT pretest probability.
management: Identify and remove the underlying cause, stopping all potentially culprit drugs including herbal and over-the-counter preparations and treating any precipitating infection
Treat immune thrombocytopenia with corticosteroids or intravenous immunoglobulin first line, escalating to thrombopoietin receptor agonists, rituximab or splenectomy for refractory disease
In heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, stop all heparin and anticoagulate with a non-heparin agent such as argatroban, danaparoid or fondaparinux, avoiding platelet transfusion
In thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, start urgent plasma exchange with corticosteroids, adding rituximab and caplacizumab, and avoid platelet transfusion
Reserve platelet transfusion for severe hypoproliferative thrombocytopenia or active bleeding, and control bleeding with antifibrinolytics and local measures
Monitor the peripheral blood film and counts, and undertake bone marrow examination in isolated thrombocytopenia in older patients or non-responders
Refer to haematology for diagnosis-specific therapy and for bleeding or thrombotic emergencies
